title: Earth and Space Science: Earth's Structure, Plate Tectonics, the Rock Cycle, Weather and Climate, Hazards, and the Solar System; Full Review
objectives: You will describe Earth's layers and explain how Earth's four systems (geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere) interact.
You will match each type of plate boundary to the landforms and hazards it produces and solve plate-motion and earthquake-wave rate problems.
You will explain how igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks form and use rock layers to put events in order.
You will distinguish weather from climate, read climate data, and explain the greenhouse effect and the cause of the seasons.
You will interpret natural hazard and solar system data and apply science practices in a full review of life, physical, and earth and space science.

slides.title: Earth and Space Science, Plus Your Full Science Review
slides.board:
Today you will:

  • Describe Earth's layers and its four connected systems
  • Match plate boundaries to the landforms and hazards they make; solve rate problems
  • Explain the rock cycle and read rock layers
  • Tell weather from climate; explain the greenhouse effect and the seasons
  • Read hazard and planet data, then review the whole Science test

Plan: Warm-up → 7 big ideas → practice together → your turn → GED-style questions

notes.say: This is our final week of Science, and it has two jobs. First, we learn the last content area on the test, Earth and space science, which is about one-fifth of the GED Science questions. Second, we pull the whole course together, because the other four-fifths is life science and physical science, and you will see review problems from both today. Almost every Earth and space question gives you a table, a graph, or a short reading, so the same skills you have built all course still do most of the work.
ask: What natural events have you lived through or seen in the news: hurricanes, floods, earthquakes, droughts? (expected answer: any; we will come back to how science explains them)

slides.title: Warm-Up: Energy and Waves Review
slides.board:
1. A 2 kg ball rolls at 3 m/s. Find its kinetic energy. (KE = ½mv2)
  2. The Sun warms Earth across empty space. Conduction, convection, or radiation?
  3. A wave has a frequency of 5 Hz and a wavelength of 2 m. Find its speed. (v = f × λ)
  4. A 12-volt battery runs a circuit with 4 Ω of resistance. Find the current. (V = IR)
steps: 1. KE = ½ × 2 × 32 = ½ × 2 × 9 = 9 J. (Square the speed first.)
2. Radiation. Only electromagnetic waves can carry energy through empty space; conduction and convection need matter.
3. v = 5 Hz × 2 m = 10 m/s.
4. I = V ÷ R = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 A.

notes.say: These four problems review last week: energy, heat transfer, waves, and circuits. Give yourself about three minutes, then tell me each answer before I reveal it. Two of these ideas come back today: radiation is how the Sun's energy reaches Earth and drives weather, and convection is what slowly moves the rock in Earth's mantle.
ask: In problem 1, what do you do first? (expected answer: square the speed, 3 squared is 9)
Why can't conduction carry the Sun's energy to Earth? (expected answer: conduction needs touching matter, and space is nearly empty)
notes.watch: On problem 1, the most common wrong answer is 3 J (forgetting to square) or 18 J (squaring 2 × 3 = 6 and halving: 36 ÷ 2). Have the student write v2 = 9 before anything else.

slides.title: Big Idea 1: Earth's Layers and Systems
slides.board:
Layers (outside in): crust (thin, solid) → mantle (thickest; solid rock that flows very slowly) → outer core (liquid iron and nickel) → inner core (solid iron and nickel; hottest, but pressure keeps it solid).

Four systems: geosphere (rock), hydrosphere (water and ice), atmosphere (air), biosphere (living things). A change in one ripples into the others.

figure.alt: Cross-section of Earth showing, from outside in: a thin solid crust, a thick mantle of solid rock that flows slowly, a liquid outer core, and a solid inner core at the center.

notes.say: Picture Earth as a peach: a thin skin, a thick fleshy middle, and a pit with two parts. The crust is the skin we live on. The mantle is the thick middle; it is solid rock, but it is so hot that over millions of years it flows like very stiff putty. The outer core is the only liquid layer, and its moving metal makes Earth's magnetic field. The inner core is the hottest place of all, yet the crushing pressure keeps it solid. Then we look at Earth a second way: as four systems that constantly trade matter and energy.
ask: Which layer is liquid? (expected answer: the outer core)
Name the system for a lake, a cloud of volcanic ash, and a forest. (expected answer: hydrosphere; atmosphere, since the ash is now in the air; biosphere)
notes.watch: Many students believe the mantle is an ocean of liquid magma. Correct it now: the mantle is solid rock that flows very slowly. Magma forms only in certain places, such as above sinking plates or at hot spots.

slides.title: Worked Example: Follow a Change Through Earth's Systems
slides.board:
A hurricane pushes a wall of seawater onto a coast. The water washes away part of a beach and leaves salt in the soil of a nearby marsh, and many marsh plants die.

Name the system at each link of the chain.
steps: The hurricane is a storm of moving air: atmosphere.
The storm pushes seawater onto land: the atmosphere acts on the hydrosphere.
The water washes away sand from the beach: the hydrosphere acts on the geosphere (erosion).
Salt in the soil kills marsh plants: the geosphere and hydrosphere act on the biosphere.
So one event touched all four systems: atmosphere → hydrosphere → geosphere → biosphere.

notes.say: GED questions often describe a chain like this and ask which systems interact, or what happens next. The method is simple: break the story into links, and for each link ask what is acting and what is being changed. Notice that the arrows go from cause to effect, just like a food chain shows where energy goes.
ask: What would happen to the animals that eat those marsh plants? (expected answer: they lose food, so their numbers may fall; the biosphere change spreads)

slides.title: Big Idea 2: Plate Tectonics
slides.board:
The crust and top of the mantle are broken into plates that move a few cm per year, driven by heat (convection) in the mantle.

BoundaryMotionWhat forms
Divergentapartmid-ocean ridges, rift valleys, new crust
Convergenttogetherocean under continent: trench, volcanoes, strong quakes; continent + continent: tall mountains
Transformslide pastearthquakes along faults, few or no volcanoes

notes.say: Plates move about as fast as your fingernails grow, a few centimeters a year, carried along by slow convection in the mantle, the same heat transfer you reviewed in the warm-up. Most earthquakes, volcanoes, and mountain ranges sit along plate edges. Learn the three boundaries by their motion: apart, together, sliding past. Then learn what each one builds. The evidence that plates move includes matching fossils and rocks on continents now separated by oceans, the puzzle fit of South America and Africa, and sea floor that is youngest at the mid-ocean ridges.
ask: What kind of boundary built the Himalayas? (expected answer: convergent, two continental plates colliding)
Why are there few volcanoes at a transform boundary? (expected answer: no plate is sinking or pulling apart, so little magma forms)
notes.watch: Students often link every volcano to divergent boundaries because "magma comes up when plates separate." That is true at ridges, but the explosive chains of volcanoes on land (the Andes, the Cascades) form where an ocean plate sinks at a convergent boundary.

slides.title: Worked Example: How Far Does a Plate Move?
slides.board:
A plate moves about 5 cm per year. How far will it move in 1 million years? Give the answer in kilometers.

distance = rate × time    100 cm = 1 m    1,000 m = 1 km
steps: distance = 5 cm/year × 1,000,000 years = 5,000,000 cm
Convert to meters: 5,000,000 cm ÷ 100 = 50,000 m
Convert to kilometers: 50,000 m ÷ 1,000 = 50 km
Check: tiny yearly motion adds up over geologic time. 50 km in a million years is reasonable.

notes.say: This is the most common calculation in Earth science questions: distance equals rate times time, with a unit change. Do the multiplication first, then convert one step at a time: centimeters to meters, then meters to kilometers. If you need the time instead, divide distance by rate, but convert the distance into the same unit as the rate first.
ask: How long would it take this plate to move 1 meter? (expected answer: 1 m = 100 cm; 100 ÷ 5 = 20 years)
notes.watch: The usual error is converting only once, giving 50,000 (meters, labeled as km), or not converting at all, giving 5,000,000. Have the student write the unit after every number.

slides.title: We Do: Boundaries and Earthquake Waves
slides.board:
1. Offshore there is a deep trench; inland there is a chain of volcanoes; strong earthquakes are common. Which boundary?
  2. An earthquake sends out P-waves (6 km/s) and S-waves (3.5 km/s) at the same moment. A station is 420 km away. How many seconds after the P-waves do the S-waves arrive?
steps: 1. Trench + volcanoes + strong quakes = convergent: an ocean plate sinking under a continental plate.
2. P-wave time: 420 ÷ 6 = 70 s.
S-wave time: 420 ÷ 3.5 = 120 s.
Gap: 120 − 70 = 50 seconds.

notes.say: Let's do these together. For the first, match features to the table: a trench means one plate is diving under another. For the second, this is the same speed formula you used in physics, time equals distance divided by speed, used twice. Seismologists use exactly this gap: the longer the wait between the two waves, the farther away the earthquake.
ask: What do you calculate first in problem 2? (expected answer: the travel time of each wave separately)
What do you do with the two times? (expected answer: subtract to find the gap)
notes.answer: 1. Convergent (ocean plate sinking beneath a continental plate). 2. P: 70 s; S: 120 s; gap 50 s.
notes.watch: Students sometimes divide 420 by the difference in speeds (6 − 3.5 = 2.5), getting 168 s. Speeds do not subtract that way; find each time separately, then subtract the times.

slides.title: Big Idea 3: The Rock Cycle and Rock Layers
slides.board:
• Igneous: melted rock (magma or lava) cools and hardens.
  • Sedimentary: weathered bits settle in layers, then are pressed and cemented. Fossils are found here.
  • Metamorphic: any rock changed by heat and pressure without melting.

Reading layers: undisturbed layers are oldest at the bottom (superposition). Rock that cuts across layers is younger than the layers it cuts.

notes.say: Rocks are recycled, slowly. Weathering breaks rock into pieces, erosion carries them away, and deposition drops them in layers that can harden into sedimentary rock. Bury and squeeze any rock hard enough and it becomes metamorphic; melt it and it cools into igneous rock. There is no fixed order: any rock type can become any other. Rock layers are also a timeline. A stack of sediment builds from the bottom up, so the bottom layer is oldest. And if magma squeezes up through layers and hardens, it must be younger than everything it cuts.
ask: Sandstone is buried deep and heated until it changes into quartzite without melting. Which rock type is quartzite? (expected answer: metamorphic)
Why are fossils rarely found in igneous rock? (expected answer: igneous rock forms from melted rock, which would destroy remains)
notes.watch: Watch for "metamorphic rock forms when rock melts." Melting leads to igneous rock. The key phrase for metamorphic is heat and pressure without melting.

slides.title: Worked Example: Put the Events in Order
slides.board: Layers A, B, C, and D are sedimentary rock. E is igneous rock that cut through some layers. List the events from oldest to youngest.

figure.alt: Rock layers stacked from bottom to top: Layer A, Layer B, Layer C, Layer D. A band of igneous rock labeled E cuts upward through Layer A, Layer B, Layer C and stops at the bottom of Layer D.

steps: Superposition: the sedimentary layers formed from the bottom up, so A, then B, then C, then D.
E cuts through A, B, and C, so E is younger than all three.
E stops at the bottom of D, so D formed on top after E hardened.
Order: A, B, C, E, D.

notes.say: Read the picture in two passes. First, stack the layers from the bottom up; that is the order they were deposited. Second, find anything that cuts across layers. Whatever it cuts is older than it, and whatever lies unbroken on top of it is younger. Say the reasoning out loud each time, because GED questions on rock layers are really questions about evidence.
ask: If E went all the way to the top surface, cutting D too, what would the order be? (expected answer: A, B, C, D, E)
notes.watch: A common mistake is listing E last just because it "looks newest." Point to the top of E: layer D lies on top of it unbroken, so D came later.

slides.title: We Do: Name That Rock
slides.board:
1. Lava pours out of a volcano and hardens within days.
  2. Mud settles at the bottom of a lake, is buried for millions of years, and hardens into shale.
  3. The shale is squeezed by colliding plates and becomes slate, without melting.
  4. Which of these three rocks could contain a fossil fish from the lake?
steps: 1. Cooled lava: igneous.
2. Buried, pressed layers of mud: sedimentary (shale).
3. Heat and pressure without melting: metamorphic (slate).
4. The shale. Fossils form in sedimentary layers; lava would destroy remains, and metamorphism usually distorts or destroys fossils.

notes.say: Talk me through each one. For every description, find the key process: cooling from melted rock, settling and cementing, or heat and pressure without melting. Problems 2 and 3 show the cycle in action: the same material changed type.
ask: What would happen if the slate were pushed even deeper and melted? (expected answer: it becomes magma; when it cools, igneous rock)
notes.watch: If the student calls slate sedimentary because it came from shale, ask: "What happened to it last?" The last process names the rock.

slides.title: Your Turn: Inside Earth and Moving Plates
slides.board:
1. Earthquake S-waves cannot travel through liquid. Which layer blocks them?
  2. A plate moves 2 cm per year. How many years will it take to move 1 km?
  3. Plates on the two sides of a long fault slide past each other. There are frequent earthquakes but no volcanoes. Which boundary?
steps: 1. The outer core, the only liquid layer.
2. 1 km = 1,000 m = 100,000 cm. 100,000 ÷ 2 = 50,000 years.
3. Transform boundary.

notes.say: Work these alone; you have four minutes. On the rate problem, convert first and write the units. Tell me your answers and how you got them before I reveal anything.
notes.watch: On problem 2, a student who converts only to meters gets 500 years. Ask: "What unit is the rate in?" Centimeters, so the distance must be in centimeters too.

slides.title: Big Idea 4: Weather, Climate, and the Greenhouse Effect
slides.board:
Weather: conditions over hours or days. Climate: the average pattern over many years (usually 30+). Climate is what you expect; weather is what you get.

The Sun drives both. The water cycle: evaporation → condensation → precipitation → collection.

Greenhouse effect: CO2, methane, and water vapor absorb heat from Earth's surface and keep Earth warm. More of these gases traps more heat.

figure.title: Carbon Dioxide in the Air at Mauna Loa, Hawaii

notes.say: Weather is today; climate is the long-term average. One cold week does not change a climate, and one hot day does not prove a warming trend; only long records can show that. The greenhouse effect itself is natural and necessary: without it, Earth would be far below freezing. The issue is the amount. The graph shows real measurements from Mauna Loa in Hawaii: carbon dioxide has climbed every decade since 1960, mainly from burning fossil fuels, and more carbon dioxide means more heat held near the surface.
ask: Weather or climate: "This city averages 50 inches of rain a year"? (expected answer: climate, a long-term average)
What does a greenhouse gas do with heat? (expected answer: it absorbs heat given off by Earth's surface and sends some back down)
notes.watch: Students confuse the greenhouse effect with the ozone hole. Ozone blocks ultraviolet light; it is a different issue. Greenhouse gases trap heat (infrared).

slides.title: Worked Example: Coastal vs. Inland Climate
slides.board:
CityMean Jan. temp (°C)Mean July temp (°C)
Coastal City (on the ocean)1022
Inland City (same latitude)−430

Find each city's yearly range. Which climate is milder, and why?

Illustrative data.
steps: Coastal range: 22 − 10 = 12°C.
Inland range: 30 − (−4) = 30 + 4 = 34°C.
The coastal city has the smaller range, so its climate is milder.
Why: water has a high specific heat. The ocean warms and cools slowly, keeping nearby air cooler in summer and warmer in winter.

notes.say: This one ties Earth science to physical science. Find each range by subtracting January from July; watch the negative sign. Then explain the pattern with a physical idea you already know: water takes a lot of energy to change temperature. And notice these are monthly means over many years, so this table describes climate, not weather.
ask: Does this table show weather or climate? (expected answer: climate; the numbers are long-term averages)
notes.watch: The trap is 30 − 4 = 26. Subtracting a negative number adds: 30 − (−4) = 34.

slides.title: Worked Example: Read the Carbon Dioxide Graph
slides.board:
Mauna Loa CO2 (parts per million): 1960: 317   1980: 339   2000: 370   2020: 414

(a) By how much did CO2 rise from 1960 to 2020? (b) What was the average rise per year? (c) Is the rise steady or speeding up?

Source: NOAA, annual means rounded.

figure.title: Carbon Dioxide in the Air at Mauna Loa, Hawaii

steps: (a) 414 − 317 = 97 ppm.
(b) 97 ppm ÷ 60 years ≈ 1.6 ppm per year.
(c) Compare equal 20-year spans: 1960–1980: 339 − 317 = 22. 2000–2020: 414 − 370 = 44.
The later 20 years rose twice as much, so the rise is speeding up, not steady.

notes.say: To describe a trend, compare equal time spans. A steady rise would add about the same amount every 20 years. Here the amount doubled, which is why the line on the graph gets steeper toward the right. This is a conclusion the data support. What the graph alone cannot tell us is the cause; we know the main cause from other evidence, like measurements of fuel burned.
ask: Why divide by 60 and not by 7? (expected answer: we want per year, and 60 years passed; 7 is the number of data points)
notes.watch: Watch for dividing by the number of points on the graph. A rate per year divides by years elapsed.

slides.title: Big Idea 5: Seasons, Days, and the Moon
slides.board:
• Rotation (spin, once a day) → day and night.
  • Revolution (orbit, once a year) + Earth's 23.5° tilt → seasons. The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun gets more direct light and longer days: summer.
  • Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January.
  • Moon phases: we see different amounts of the Moon's sunlit half as it orbits Earth (about 29.5 days).

notes.say: Here is the most famous misconception in all of Earth science: that summer happens because Earth is closer to the Sun. If that were true, both hemispheres would have summer at the same time, and they do not. In July, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, so sunlight hits it more directly and days are long; at the same moment, Australia is tilted away and has winter. Direct light matters because the same beam of energy is concentrated on a smaller area. The Moon works by the same idea of viewing angle: half of it is always lit, and the phase is how much of that lit half faces us.
ask: If it is summer in the United States, what season is it in Argentina? (expected answer: winter)
What causes day and night? (expected answer: Earth's rotation on its axis)
notes.watch: Also watch for "phases are Earth's shadow." Earth's shadow on the Moon is a lunar eclipse, which is rare. Phases happen every month.

slides.title: We Do: Explain the Seasons
slides.board:
1. Earth is about 3% closer to the Sun in January than in July. Why is January still winter in the Northern Hemisphere?
  2. In December, is the Southern Hemisphere tilted toward or away from the Sun? What season does it have?
  3. A city near the equator has nearly 12 hours of daylight all year. Why are its seasons weak?
steps: 1. The Northern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun in January: slanted light and short days. Tilt matters far more than a 3% change in distance.
2. Tilted toward the Sun, so it has summer.
3. Near the equator, sunlight stays fairly direct all year and day length barely changes, so the tilt has little effect.

notes.say: Let's reason through these together using one idea: the angle of sunlight and the length of the day. Each time, ask which hemisphere leans toward the Sun at that time of year.
ask: What two things make summer warmer? (expected answer: more direct sunlight and longer days)
notes.answer: 1. Tilt away from the Sun: less direct light, shorter days. 2. Toward; summer. 3. Sun angle and day length change little near the equator.
notes.watch: If a student falls back on distance, point to problem 1: distance is smallest in January, during northern winter. The data rule it out.

slides.title: Big Idea 6: Natural Hazards
slides.board:
Earthquakes, volcanoes, tsunamis, landslides, hurricanes, tornadoes, floods, droughts. We cannot stop them; we reduce harm with monitoring, warnings, building codes, and land-use planning.

Earthquake magnitude: each +1 = 10× the shaking (wave amplitude) and about 32× the energy.

Hurricane category12345
Wind (mph)74–9596–110111–129130–156157+

notes.say: Natural hazards are where Earth science meets daily life. Earthquakes and volcanoes come from plate motion; hurricanes, floods, and droughts come from the atmosphere and the water cycle. The magnitude scale is the one number trick to master: it multiplies. Going up one step means ten times the shaking and about thirty-two times the energy, so a magnitude 7 is not slightly bigger than a 6. The hurricane table is the Saffir-Simpson scale used by the National Hurricane Center; you only need to read it, not memorize it.
ask: A hurricane has sustained winds of 115 mph. What category? (expected answer: Category 3)
Name one way people reduce earthquake damage. (expected answer: stronger building codes, warning systems, avoiding building on unstable ground)
notes.watch: Students treat magnitude like ordinary counting: "a 6 is twice a 3." Make them write the multiplication: 6 − 3 = 3 steps, so 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000 times the shaking.

slides.title: Worked Example: Compare Two Earthquakes
slides.board:
Earthquake A has magnitude 7.0. Earthquake B has magnitude 5.0.

(a) How many times greater is A's shaking? (b) About how many times more energy does A release?
steps: Find the difference: 7.0 − 5.0 = 2 steps.
(a) Shaking: 10 × 10 = 102 = 100 times.
(b) Energy: 32 × 32 = 1,024, or about 1,000 times.
So a magnitude 7 is not "a little more than a 5": it releases about a thousand times the energy.

notes.say: Always start with the difference in magnitude, because that tells you how many times to multiply. Then multiply by 10 for shaking or by about 32 for energy, once for each step. Your calculator's power key helps: 10 to the power of the difference.
ask: How much more shaking does a magnitude 6.0 have than a 4.0? (expected answer: 2 steps, 100 times)
notes.watch: Watch for 20 (10 × 2) or 2 (just the difference). Each step is a multiplication, not an addition.

slides.title: Big Idea 7: The Solar System and the Universe
slides.board:
• The Sun is a star; its gravity holds 8 planets in orbit.
  • Inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars): small and rocky. Outer planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune): huge, mostly gas and ice.
  • Farther from the Sun → longer orbit (longer year).
  • Our Sun is one star in the Milky Way galaxy, one of billions of galaxies. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year (about 9.5 trillion km).
  • Universe: about 13.8 billion years old (Big Bang). Earth: about 4.6 billion.

notes.say: Space questions on the GED are mostly data questions: a planet table, and a question about the pattern or the exception. The big pattern is that the farther a planet is from the Sun, the longer its year and, usually, the colder it is. The famous exception is Venus, which is hotter than Mercury because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere creates an extreme greenhouse effect, which links back to Big Idea 4. Gravity is the force behind all of it: it holds the planets in orbit, holds the Moon around Earth, and pulled gas and dust together to form the Sun and planets.
ask: What is a light-year a measure of: time or distance? (expected answer: distance)
What force keeps Earth in orbit? (expected answer: the Sun's gravity)
notes.watch: "Light-year" sounds like time. Stress that it is a distance, used because space distances are too large for kilometers to be practical.

ask: Would you predict Jupiter's year to be longer or shorter than Mars's? (expected answer: longer, it is farther from the Sun; it is about 11.9 Earth years)

slides.title: Your Turn: Climate, Hazards, and Space
slides.board:
1. Weather or climate: "Summers in this valley are usually hot and dry."
  2. How many times greater is the shaking of a magnitude 6.0 earthquake than a magnitude 3.0?
  3. A hurricane has sustained winds of 140 mph. What category is it?
  4. Why is Venus hotter than Mercury?
steps: 1. Climate: it describes the usual, long-term pattern.
2. 6.0 − 3.0 = 3 steps; 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000 times.
3. 140 mph falls in 130–156: Category 4.
4. Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat: a runaway greenhouse effect.

notes.say: Four quick problems, one from each of the last four big ideas. You have four minutes. Commit to your answers and tell me how you decided before I reveal them.
notes.answer: 1. Climate. 2. 1,000 times. 3. Category 4. 4. Its thick CO2 atmosphere creates a strong greenhouse effect.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Which Boundary?
slides.board:
Scientists map a region with these features: a deep ocean trench just offshore, a line of active volcanoes about 200 km inland, and earthquakes that occur deeper and deeper the farther inland they are.

Which explanation best fits the evidence?

A. Two plates are moving apart, and magma rises to fill the gap.
B. Two continental plates are colliding head-on, crumpling the crust.
C. An ocean plate is sinking beneath a continental plate.
D. Two plates are sliding horizontally past each other along a fault.
steps: A is out. Plates moving apart make ridges and rift valleys, not a deep trench, and their earthquakes stay shallow.
B is out. Two continents colliding build tall mountains but produce few volcanoes, and there is no ocean trench.
D is out. Sliding plates make earthquakes along a fault but no trench and few or no volcanoes.
C is correct. The sinking plate forms the trench; as it dives deeper inland, earthquakes get deeper along it, and melting above it feeds the volcanoes.

notes.say: This question gives you three clues and asks you to match them to a boundary. Treat each clue as a test that the right answer must pass. The deepening earthquakes are the strongest clue: they trace the path of a plate sliding down into the mantle.
ask: Which clue rules out a transform boundary fastest? (expected answer: the trench, or the volcanoes)
notes.answer: C. A trench, inland volcanoes, and earthquakes that deepen inland are the signature of an ocean plate sinking beneath a continental plate.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Life Science Review
slides.board:
Light-colored beetles lived on pale sand on an island. After an eruption covered the island in dark ash, birds ate more light beetles than dark beetles. Ten years later, most beetles on the island were dark.

Which statement best explains the change?

A. The beetles darkened their bodies during their lives to match the ash.
B. Dark beetles survived and reproduced more, passing on the dark trait.
C. The ash caused new mutations for dark color in every beetle.
D. Birds learned to prefer the taste of light beetles.
steps: A is out. Individuals do not change their inherited color to fit their surroundings; populations change over generations.
C is out. Mutations are random and rare; ash does not give every beetle a dark-color gene. The dark trait was already present.
D is out. Nothing in the passage says taste changed. Birds caught light beetles more easily because they stood out on dark ash.
B is correct. This is natural selection: variation already existed, dark beetles were better hidden, so they survived, reproduced, and passed on the trait.

notes.say: Here is a review question from Week 6 that starts with an Earth event. A volcanic eruption changed the geosphere, and that changed which beetles survived in the biosphere. Use the four conditions of natural selection: variation, inheritance, overproduction, and selection.
ask: What earth-system interaction starts this story? (expected answer: geosphere to biosphere, ash changing the beetles' habitat)
notes.answer: B. Natural selection: dark beetles were already present, survived better on dark ash, and passed the trait to offspring.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Physical Science Review
slides.board:
A student mixes 10.0 g of baking soda with 50.0 g of vinegar in an open cup. The mixture fizzes. Afterward the cup's contents have a mass of 55.6 g.

Which statement best explains the lower mass?

A. The reaction destroyed 4.4 g of matter.
B. A gas formed in the reaction and escaped into the air.
C. The scale is wrong, because mass can never change in a reaction.
D. The baking soda dissolved, and dissolved matter has no mass.
steps: A is out. Matter is not created or destroyed in a chemical reaction (conservation of mass).
C is out. The total mass is conserved, but the mass in the open cup can drop when something leaves it. No error is needed.
D is out. Dissolved substances still have mass; sugar water weighs more than plain water.
B is correct. The fizzing is carbon dioxide gas. 60.0 − 55.6 = 4.4 g of gas escaped. In a sealed container the mass would stay 60.0 g.

notes.say: This review question is from Week 7, chemistry. Conservation of mass says total mass stays the same in a reaction, but only if you count everything. An open cup lets gas leave, so the cup gets lighter while the total does not change.
ask: How much gas escaped? (expected answer: 60.0 minus 55.6 = 4.4 g)
notes.answer: B. Carbon dioxide gas (4.4 g) escaped from the open cup; mass was conserved overall.

screens.title: What you will learn
screens.html:
About one-fifth of the GED Science test is Earth and space science. Those questions almost always give you a table, graph, or short reading, so you need the big ideas and the same data skills you have practiced all course. This is also your final science lesson, so it ends with a review of life science and physical science, which make up the other four-fifths of the test. In this lesson you will:

  • Describe Earth's layers and its four connected systems.
  • Match each plate boundary to what it builds, and solve plate-motion rate problems.
  • Explain how igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks form, and read rock layers.
  • Tell weather from climate, and explain the greenhouse effect and the seasons.
  • Read natural hazard and solar system data.
  • Review the key tools from the whole Science course.

Each screen teaches one idea and ends with a quick check.

screens.title: Earth's layers
screens.html:
If you could slice Earth in half, you would see four layers. From the outside in:

  • Crust: thin, solid rock. It is the layer we live on, about 5 to 70 km thick.
  • Mantle: the thickest layer, nearly 2,900 km. It is hot, solid rock that flows very slowly, like extremely stiff putty, over millions of years.
  • Outer core: liquid iron and nickel. Its flowing metal produces Earth's magnetic field.
  • Inner core: solid iron and nickel. It is the hottest layer, but enormous pressure keeps it solid.

Temperature and pressure both rise as you go deeper. Remember: only one layer, the outer core, is liquid.

options: It is hot, solid rock that flows very slowly over long periods.
It is an ocean of liquid magma lying just beneath the crust.
It is the thinnest layer, found just beneath the floor of the ocean.
It is liquid iron and nickel whose motion creates the magnetic field.
why: This is the most common misconception about Earth's interior. The mantle is solid rock; magma forms only in certain places, such as above a sinking plate.
That describes the crust, which is the thinnest layer. The mantle is the thickest layer, nearly 2,900 km thick.
That describes the outer core. The mantle is made of rock, not liquid metal.
check.hint: Only one layer is liquid, and it is not the mantle.
check.explain: The mantle is the thickest layer and is made of hot, solid rock that flows very slowly. The tempting answer, "an ocean of liquid magma," is a misconception: the only liquid layer is the outer core, which is metal, not rock.

screens.title: Earth's four systems
screens.html:
Scientists also think of Earth as four connected systems:

  • Geosphere: rock, soil, and Earth's interior.
  • Hydrosphere: all water: oceans, rivers, groundwater, and ice.
  • Atmosphere: the layer of gases around Earth.
  • Biosphere: all living things.

A change in one system ripples into the others. GED questions often describe a chain of events and ask which systems interact or what happens next. Break the story into links and name the system at each link.

example.prompt: A volcano erupts and sends ash high into the air. The ash blocks some sunlight for months, and crops grow poorly. Name the systems in order.
steps: The volcano and its ash come from Earth's interior: geosphere.
Ash spreads high in the air and blocks sunlight: atmosphere.
Crops grow poorly with less sunlight: biosphere.

check.prompt: Sort each part of Earth into the system it belongs to.
choices: Nitrogen and oxygen gas around Earth
check.why: The most common mistake is putting glacier ice in the geosphere because it is solid. The hydrosphere includes all of Earth's water, frozen or liquid.
check.hint: Ask: is it rock, water (in any form), air, or alive?
check.explain: Geosphere: the granite mountain. Hydrosphere: groundwater and glacier ice (all water, including ice). Atmosphere: nitrogen and oxygen gas, and wind (moving air). Biosphere: the living corals.

screens.title: Plate tectonics
screens.html:
Earth's crust and the rigid top of the mantle are broken into huge pieces called tectonic plates. Heat from Earth's interior drives slow convection currents in the mantle, and the plates move a few centimeters per year, about as fast as your fingernails grow. Most earthquakes, volcanoes, and mountain ranges are found along plate edges.

Evidence that plates move:

  • Matching fossils and rock types on continents now separated by oceans.
  • The puzzle-like fit of South America and Africa.
  • Sea floor that is youngest at mid-ocean ridges and older farther away.
  • Earthquakes and volcanoes lined up along plate edges.

check.prompt: Which observation is evidence that continents have moved over time?
options: Fossils of one freshwater reptile appear in both South America and Africa.
The oldest rocks on the sea floor are found right along the mid-ocean ridges.
Mountain ranges are slowly worn down by wind, rain, and ice over millions of years.
Earth's liquid outer core produces a magnetic field that surrounds the planet.
why: This reverses the evidence. New sea floor forms at the ridges, so the youngest rocks are there, and rocks get older moving away from them.
This describes weathering and erosion. It is true, but it says nothing about continents changing position.
This is a true fact about the core, but it is not evidence that continents moved.
check.hint: Look for an observation that only makes sense if two continents were once joined.
check.explain: A small freshwater reptile could not swim across an ocean. Finding its fossils on two continents now far apart is best explained if the continents were once joined and later moved apart. The statement about the oldest sea floor at the ridges is backward: the youngest sea floor is at the ridges.

screens.title: Plate boundaries
screens.html:
What happens at a boundary depends on how the plates move:

BoundaryPlates…What forms
Divergentmove apartMid-ocean ridges, rift valleys, new crust from rising magma
Convergentpush togetherOcean plate under continent: deep trench, chain of volcanoes, strong earthquakes. Continent with continent: tall mountains, few volcanoes
Transformslide past each otherEarthquakes along faults; few or no volcanoes

example.prompt: The Himalayas are the tallest mountains on Earth. They have frequent earthquakes but few volcanoes. What kind of boundary formed them?
steps: Tall mountains mean crust is being pushed together and crumpled: convergent.
Few volcanoes means no ocean plate is sinking and melting; both plates are continental.
example.answer: A convergent boundary where two continental plates collide.

check.prompt:
Complete the statements.

At a {{0}} boundary, plates move apart and new crust forms. Where two plates slide past each other at a transform boundary, the main hazard is {{1}}.

options: divergent
convergent
transform
why: At a convergent boundary plates push together; crust is destroyed or crumpled, not created.
At a transform boundary plates slide sideways past each other; crust is neither created nor destroyed.

options: earthquakes
volcanic eruptions
new mountain chains
why: Transform boundaries have few or no volcanoes, because no plate sinks and melts there.
Tall mountain chains form where plates push together, not where they slide past each other.

check.hint: Apart = divergent; together = convergent; sliding past = transform.
check.explain: Plates move apart at a divergent boundary, where rising magma forms new crust. At a transform boundary the plates grind sideways, building up stress that is released as earthquakes; there are few or no volcanoes.

screens.title: Rates of plate motion
screens.html:
Plate motion problems use the same formula as speed problems:

distance = rate × time     time = distance ÷ rate

The trick is units. Rates are usually in centimeters per year, but distances may be in meters or kilometers. Convert to the rate's unit first.

  • 100 cm = 1 m
  • 1,000 m = 1 km, so 1 km = 100,000 cm

example.prompt: The Atlantic Ocean widens about 2.5 cm per year. How much wider will it be in 100 years, in meters?
steps: distance = 2.5 cm/year × 100 years = 250 cm
250 cm ÷ 100 = 2.5 m

check.prompt: A plate moves 3 cm per year. How many years will it take to move 1.5 meters?

mistakes.why: You divided 1.5 by 3 without converting. The rate is in centimeters, so change 1.5 m to 150 cm first: 150 ÷ 3 = 50.
You multiplied the distance by the rate. To find time, divide distance by rate, after converting 1.5 m to 150 cm.
You converted to 150 cm but then multiplied by 3. Time = distance ÷ rate = 150 ÷ 3 = 50.

check.hint: Change meters to centimeters, then divide by the rate.
check.explain:
1.5 m × 100 = 150 cm.

time = distance ÷ rate = 150 cm ÷ 3 cm per year = 50 years.

screens.title: The rock cycle
screens.html:
Rocks are slowly recycled from one type to another:

  • Igneous rock forms when melted rock cools and hardens: magma underground (cooling slowly, big crystals, like granite) or lava at the surface (cooling fast, tiny crystals, like basalt).
  • Sedimentary rock forms when weathering breaks rock into bits, erosion carries them away, and they settle in layers that are pressed and cemented. Sandstone, shale, and limestone are examples. Fossils are found here.
  • Metamorphic rock forms when any rock is changed by heat and pressure without melting. Limestone becomes marble; shale becomes slate.

There is no fixed order. Any rock can be weathered, buried and squeezed, or melted.

example.prompt: Trace one path through the cycle: granite on a mountain becomes sand on a beach, then sandstone, then quartzite.
steps: Granite (igneous) is weathered into sand grains, which are eroded and carried to the beach.
The sand is buried, pressed, and cemented: sandstone (sedimentary).
The sandstone is buried deeper and changed by heat and pressure without melting: quartzite (metamorphic).

check.prompt: Deep underground, limestone is heated and squeezed by colliding plates. It changes into marble without melting. What type of rock is marble?
options: Metamorphic rock
Igneous rock
Sedimentary rock
Magma
why: Igneous rock forms only from melted rock that cools. The limestone did not melt.
Limestone, the starting rock, is sedimentary. But the rock is named for what happened to it last: heat and pressure made it metamorphic.
Magma is melted rock. The prompt says the limestone did not melt.
check.hint: Heat and pressure without melting is the key phrase.
check.explain: Any rock changed by heat and pressure without melting becomes metamorphic rock. Marble started as sedimentary limestone, but its type is named for its most recent change.

screens.title: Reading rock layers
screens.html:
Rock layers are a record of Earth's history. Two rules let you put events in order:

  • Superposition: in undisturbed sedimentary layers, the oldest layer is at the bottom and the youngest is at the top, because layers pile up from the bottom.
  • Cross-cutting: rock that cuts across other layers is younger than the layers it cuts. (You cannot cut through something that is not there yet.)

Fossils in a layer are about the same age as the layer, so fossils in lower layers are generally older.

In the diagram, layers P, Q, R, and S are sedimentary. T is igneous rock that squeezed up as magma and hardened.

check.prompt: Look at the diagram. Which list puts the events in order from oldest to youngest?
options: P, Q, T, R, S
P, Q, R, S, T
S, R, Q, P, T
T, P, Q, R, S
why: You put T last because it cuts across layers. But T stops at the bottom of R, and R and S lie unbroken on top of it, so R and S formed after T.
This reverses superposition. In undisturbed layers the bottom layer, P, is the oldest, not the youngest.
You put T first because it reaches the bottom of the diagram. T cuts through P and Q, so it must be younger than both.
check.hint: Stack the layers from the bottom up. Then ask: which layers does T cut, and which lie on top of it?
check.explain: By superposition, P formed first, then Q. T cuts through P and Q, so it is younger than both. T stops at the bottom of R, so R (and then S) were deposited after T hardened. Order: P, Q, T, R, S. Putting T last is the tempting error: it only cuts P and Q.

screens.title: Weather, climate, and the water cycle
screens.html:
Weather is the condition of the air at a place over hours or days: today's temperature, rain, wind. Climate is the average pattern over many years, usually 30 or more. Climate is what you expect; weather is what you get.

The Sun drives both. Uneven heating of Earth's surface creates winds and ocean currents that carry heat from the equator toward the poles. The water cycle moves water between systems: evaporation (liquid to vapor), condensation (vapor cools into cloud droplets), precipitation (rain, snow), and collection (in oceans, lakes, and groundwater).

Clue words: today, tonight, this week, forecast point to weather. Average, usually, typical, per year point to climate.

example.prompt: A town recorded yearly rainfall of 12, 9, 14, and 13 inches over four years. What is the mean, and is it weather or climate?
steps: Mean: 48 ÷ 4 = 12 inches.
An average over years describes climate (a real climate average would use about 30 years).

options: Winters in this mountain town are usually long and snowy.
The region receives an average of 15 inches of rain per year.
A storm dropped 2 inches of rain on the town last night.
Forecasters expect strong winds and hail tomorrow afternoon.
It was 98°F at the airport at 3:00 this afternoon.
why: One night's storm is a short-term condition, so it is weather.
A forecast for tomorrow describes short-term conditions, so it is weather.
A single reading at one time on one day is weather.
check.hint: Look for words like usually and average.
check.explain: "Usually long and snowy" and "an average of 15 inches per year" describe long-term patterns, so they are climate. The other three describe one night, tomorrow, or one moment: weather.

screens.title: The greenhouse effect and climate data
screens.html:
Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms Earth's surface. The warm surface gives off heat (infrared energy). Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide (CO2), methane, and water vapor absorb much of that heat and send some back toward the surface. This natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm enough for life.

Adding more greenhouse gases, mainly by burning fossil fuels, traps more heat and raises Earth's average temperature. The graph shows real measurements of CO2 in the air at Mauna Loa, Hawaii (NOAA annual means, rounded). To describe a trend, compare equal time spans: from 1960 to 1990 CO2 rose 37 ppm; from 1990 to 2020 it rose 60 ppm. The rise is speeding up.

figure.title: Carbon Dioxide in the Air at Mauna Loa, Hawaii

check.prompt: Use the graph. By how many parts per million (ppm) did CO2 increase from 1980 to 2020?

mistakes.why: 97 is the increase from 1960 to 2020. Start at the 1980 value, 339 ppm: 414 − 339 = 75.
You found the average rise per year (75 ÷ 40). The question asks for the total increase: 414 − 339 = 75 ppm.
24 is the increase from 2010 to 2020 only. Use the 1980 value: 414 − 339 = 75.

check.hint: Read the values for 1980 and 2020, then subtract.

screens.title: Seasons, days, and the Moon
screens.html:
• Rotation: Earth spins on its axis once a day, causing day and night.
  • Revolution: Earth orbits the Sun once a year.
  • Seasons come from Earth's 23.5° tilt. The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun gets more direct sunlight (energy concentrated on a smaller area) and longer days: summer. The other hemisphere has winter at the same time.

Seasons are not caused by distance. Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during Northern Hemisphere winter.

Moon phases: half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun. As the Moon orbits Earth (about every 29.5 days), we see different amounts of that lit half. Earth's shadow on the Moon is a lunar eclipse, a rare event, not a phase.

check.prompt: Why does the Moon appear to change shape over about a month?
options: As the Moon orbits Earth, we see different amounts of its sunlit half.
Earth's shadow covers a different part of the Moon on each night of the month.
The Moon makes its own light, which brightens and dims each month.
The Moon's distance from the Sun changes greatly during each month.
why: Earth's shadow falling on the Moon is a lunar eclipse, which happens only occasionally. Phases happen every month without any shadow from Earth.
The Moon makes no light of its own; it reflects sunlight. Half of it is always lit.
This is the same distance misconception as with seasons. The Moon's distance from the Sun barely changes; what changes is our viewing angle.
check.hint: Half the Moon is always lit. What changes is how much of that lit half faces Earth.
check.explain: The Sun always lights half of the Moon. As the Moon orbits Earth, we see more or less of that lit half, which produces the phases. The tempting answer, Earth's shadow, describes a lunar eclipse.

screens.title: Natural hazards and the magnitude scale
screens.html:
Natural hazards are natural events that can harm people: earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, tsunamis, landslides, hurricanes, tornadoes, floods, and droughts. Scientists cannot prevent them, but monitoring, warning systems, building codes, and careful land-use planning reduce the harm.

Earthquake magnitude measures an earthquake's size. The scale multiplies:

Each whole number up = 10 times the ground shaking (wave amplitude) and about 32 times the energy released.

To compare two earthquakes, find the difference in magnitude, then multiply by 10 once for each step.

example.prompt: How many times greater is the shaking of a magnitude 8.0 earthquake than a magnitude 5.0?
steps: Difference: 8.0 − 5.0 = 3 steps.
Shaking: 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000.

check.prompt: How many times greater is the ground shaking of a magnitude 6.5 earthquake than a magnitude 4.5 earthquake?

mistakes.why: 2 is the difference in magnitude, the number of steps. Each step multiplies the shaking by 10: 10 × 10 = 100.
You multiplied 10 by 2. The steps multiply, not add: 10 × 10 = 100.
That is the energy comparison (32 × 32 is about 1,000). The question asks about shaking, which grows 10 times per step: 100.

check.hint: Find the difference in magnitude. Multiply by 10 that many times.

screens.title: Hurricanes and other weather hazards
screens.html:
Hurricanes form over warm ocean water, which supplies the heat and moisture that power them. They bring high winds, heavy rain, flooding, and storm surge (seawater pushed onto land). Forecasters rate hurricanes by sustained wind speed on the Saffir-Simpson scale:

CategorySustained winds (mph)
174–95
296–110
3111–129
4130–156
5157 or higher

Categories 3 to 5 are called major hurricanes. Hurricanes weaken over land or cold water because they lose their source of warm, moist air.

check.prompt: Use the table. A hurricane with sustained winds of 100 mph is Category {{0}}. If its winds increase to 135 mph, it becomes Category {{1}}.

why: Category 1 ends at 95 mph; 100 mph is above that range.
Category 3 starts at 111 mph; 100 mph is below that range.
Category 4 starts at 130 mph; 100 mph is far below it.
Category 2 ends at 110 mph; 135 mph is well above that.
Category 3 ends at 129 mph; 135 mph is above that range.
Category 5 starts at 157 mph; 135 mph is below that.

check.hint: Find the row whose range includes each wind speed.
check.explain: 100 mph falls in 96–110 mph: Category 2. 135 mph falls in 130–156 mph: Category 4.

screens.title: The solar system
screens.html:
The Sun is a medium-sized star at the center of our solar system. Its gravity holds eight planets in orbit.

  • Inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars): small and rocky.
  • Outer planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune): huge, made mostly of gas and ice, with no solid surface.

Patterns in planet data: the farther a planet is from the Sun, the longer its year (time to orbit) and usually the colder it is. The well-known exception is Venus: it is hotter than Mercury, which is closer to the Sun, because Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere creates an extreme greenhouse effect.

Planet years are often given in Earth years. To change Earth years to days, multiply by 365.

example.prompt: Mars takes 1.88 Earth years to orbit the Sun. About how many Earth days is that?
steps: Multiply by 365: 1.88 × 365 = 686.2.
About 686 days (NASA lists 687).

check.prompt: Jupiter takes 11.86 Earth years to orbit the Sun. About how many Earth days is one Jupiter year? Round to the nearest whole day.

mistakes.why: You divided 365 by 11.86. One Jupiter year is longer than an Earth year, so multiply: 11.86 × 365 = 4,329.
You added 11.86 and 365. To convert years to days, multiply: 11.86 × 365 = 4,329.

check.hint: Each Earth year has 365 days. Multiply.
check.explain: 11.86 × 365 = 4,328.9, which rounds to 4,329 days. (NASA lists 4,331 days; the small difference comes from leap years and rounding.)

screens.title: Stars, galaxies, and the universe
screens.html:
• Our Sun is one of hundreds of billions of stars in the Milky Way galaxy. A galaxy is a huge system of stars, gas, and dust held together by gravity, and the universe holds billions of galaxies.
  • Distances in space are so large that scientists use the light-year: the distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion km. Light from the Sun takes only about 8 minutes to reach Earth.
  • Evidence such as galaxies moving away from each other supports the Big Bang theory: the universe began expanding about 13.8 billion years ago.
  • Earth and the solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago, when gravity pulled a cloud of gas and dust together.

check.prompt: A star is 25 light-years from Earth. What does this mean?
options: Light leaving the star takes 25 years to travel to Earth.
The star formed about 25 years ago and is still very young.
The star is exactly 25 times as far from Earth as the Sun is.
A spacecraft from Earth would need 25 years to reach the star.
why: A light-year measures distance, not age. The name sounds like a unit of time, which is why this mix-up is common.
A light-year is not a comparison with the Sun's distance. The Sun is only about 8 light-minutes away, so 25 light-years is far more than 25 times that.
A light-year is based on the speed of light, not of spacecraft. Our spacecraft travel far slower than light and would need many thousands of years.
check.hint: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year.
check.explain: A light-year is the distance light travels in a year. A star 25 light-years away is so far that its light needs 25 years to reach us, so we see the star as it was 25 years ago. The term measures distance, not the star's age.

screens.title: Full review: life science toolkit
screens.html:
Life science is about 40% of the GED Science test. Make sure these tools feel automatic:

  • Punnett square: put one parent's alleles across the top and the other's down the side. Each of the 4 boxes is a 25% chance. A recessive trait shows only with two recessive alleles.
  • Energy in food chains: only about 10% of the energy at one level passes to the next. Multiply by 0.10 once for each arrow.
  • Photosynthesis (plants, in light): CO2 + water → sugar + oxygen. Cellular respiration (all living things, all the time): sugar + oxygen → CO2 + water + energy.
  • Natural selection: variation, inheritance, overproduction, selection. Populations change; individuals do not.

example.prompt: In pea plants, tall (T) is dominant over short (t). Two Tt plants are crossed. What is the chance of a short plant?
steps: Boxes: TT, Tt, Tt, tt.
Short needs tt: 1 box of 4.
1 ÷ 4 = 25%.

check.prompt: In an ocean food chain, algae store 40,000 kJ of energy. Tiny animals called zooplankton eat the algae, and small fish eat the zooplankton. About how many kilojoules reach the small fish?

mistakes.why: 4,000 kJ is what reaches the zooplankton after one step. The small fish are one more step up: 4,000 × 0.10 = 400.
You took 10% three times. Count the arrows: algae → zooplankton → small fish is two steps.
You subtracted 10% instead of keeping 10%. Only about 10% passes up each level: 40,000 × 0.10 × 0.10 = 400.

check.hint: Count the arrows from algae to small fish. Multiply by 0.10 for each one.

screens.title: Full review: physical science toolkit
screens.html:
Physical science (chemistry and physics) is the other 40% of the test. Know these formulas on sight. The GED gives you an on-screen calculator, and a question that needs a formula usually states it, but you must know how to set it up.

FormulaUse
speed = distance ÷ timeMotion, seismic waves, plate motion
density = mass ÷ volumeRocks, floating and sinking
force = mass × acceleration (F = ma)Newton's second law; force in newtons (N)
work = force × distanceMachines; work in joules (J)

Also remember: mass and energy are conserved. They change form but are never created or destroyed.

example.prompt: A seismic wave travels 360 km in 60 seconds. What is its speed?
steps: speed = distance ÷ time
360 km ÷ 60 s = 6 km/s

check.prompt: A 1,200 kg car speeds up at 3 m/s2. What net force, in newtons, acts on the car?

mistakes.why: You divided mass by acceleration. Newton's second law multiplies: F = ma = 1,200 × 3 = 3,600 N.
You added mass and acceleration. F = ma means multiply: 1,200 × 3 = 3,600 N.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• Layers: crust, mantle (solid, flows slowly), outer core (liquid), inner core (solid). Systems: geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere; a change in one affects the others.
  • Plates: divergent = apart (ridges, rifts); convergent = together (trenches, volcanoes, mountains); transform = slide past (earthquakes). distance = rate × time; convert units first.
  • Rocks: igneous (cooled melted rock), sedimentary (pressed layers; fossils), metamorphic (heat and pressure, no melting). Oldest layers at the bottom; rock that cuts layers is younger.
  • Weather = short-term; climate = long-term average. Greenhouse gases trap heat. Tilt causes the seasons.
  • Magnitude: +1 = 10× shaking, about 32× energy.
  • Space: gravity holds planets in orbit; farther planets have longer years; a light-year is a distance.

For every science question: read the question first, label the variables, state the pattern, find the exception, and choose the conclusion that stays inside the data.

Next, go to Practice and start with Set A. It mixes Earth and space science with review from life and physical science.
