items.prompt: Which layer of Earth is made mostly of liquid iron and nickel?
options: Outer core
Inner core
Mantle
Crust
items.hint: One of the two core layers is solid because of extreme pressure; the other is liquid.
items.explain:
The outer core is liquid iron and nickel. Its flowing metal produces Earth's magnetic field.

The inner core is made of the same metals and is even hotter, but the enormous pressure at Earth's center keeps it solid. The mantle is mostly solid rock that flows very slowly, and the crust is solid rock.
why: The inner core is made of the same metals and is even hotter, but enormous pressure at Earth's center keeps it solid.
This is the common "sea of magma" misconception. The mantle is solid rock that flows very slowly; it is not liquid.
The crust is the thin layer of solid rock we live on. It is not made of iron and nickel.

items.prompt: Which statement describes weather rather than climate?
options: A cold front brought 3 inches of snow to the city overnight.
The city averages 42 inches of precipitation in a typical year.
Winters in the region are usually mild, cloudy, and wet.
Over the past 30 years, the typical July high has been 88°F.
why: An average yearly amount is a long-term pattern, which is climate.
"Usually" signals what winters are like year after year: a long-term pattern, which is climate.
A typical value over 30 years is exactly how scientists define climate.
items.hint: Weather is about hours or days. Climate is about years.
items.explain: Snow from one cold front overnight is a short-term condition: weather. The other three describe averages or usual patterns over many years, which is climate. The 30-year July high may look like a single temperature, but "typical over 30 years" makes it climate.

items.prompt: Sort each description into the type of rock it forms.
choices: Lava from a volcano cools and hardens on the surface.
Layers of sand are buried, pressed, and cemented together.
Limestone deep underground is changed by heat and pressure without melting.
Magma cools slowly far beneath the surface.
Shells and mud settle on the sea floor and harden over time.
Shale is squeezed by colliding plates and becomes slate.
items.hint: Melted rock cooling = igneous. Layers pressed together = sedimentary. Heat and pressure without melting = metamorphic.
items.explain:
Igneous: lava cooling on the surface and magma cooling underground. Both start as melted rock.

Sedimentary: sand layers and shells and mud. Both are pieces that settle in layers and are pressed and cemented.

Metamorphic: limestone changed by heat and pressure, and shale squeezed into slate. Both are existing rocks changed without melting. If the rock had melted, it would become magma and then igneous rock.
items.why: The most common mistake is sorting "Shale is squeezed by colliding plates and becomes slate" as sedimentary because shale is sedimentary. A rock is named for its most recent change: heat and pressure without melting make slate metamorphic.

items.prompt: In pea plants, the allele for purple flowers (P) is dominant over the allele for white flowers (p). Two plants with the genotype Pp are crossed. What is the probability that an offspring plant will have white flowers?
items.hint: Draw a 2-by-2 Punnett square. White flowers need two recessive alleles.
items.explain:
Punnett square for Pp × Pp: the four boxes are PP, Pp, Pp, pp.

Only pp has two recessive alleles, so only 1 of 4 boxes shows white flowers: 1 ÷ 4 = 25%.

75% is the probability of purple flowers (PP, Pp, Pp), a common mix-up. 50% is the probability of the Pp genotype.
why: You may have reasoned that two purple parents cannot have white offspring. Each Pp parent carries a hidden p allele, so pp offspring appear in 1 of 4 boxes.
50% is the chance of the Pp genotype (2 of 4 boxes). White flowers need pp, which is only 1 box.
75% is the chance of purple flowers (PP, Pp, Pp). The question asks about white, which is the one pp box.

items.prompt: Scientists study a newly mapped boundary where an ocean plate is sinking beneath a continental plate. Based on the table, which set of features would they most likely find there?
options: A deep ocean trench, a chain of volcanoes, and strong earthquakes
Very tall mountains, frequent earthquakes, and few volcanoes
An underwater ridge where new sea floor is forming
Frequent earthquakes along a fault, with no volcanoes
items.hint: Find the row in the table with the same plate motion.
items.explain:
The west coast of South America is the row where an ocean plate sinks beneath a continental plate. Its features are a deep trench, a chain of volcanoes, and strong earthquakes, so a boundary with the same motion would most likely have the same features.

Tall mountains with few volcanoes match two continental plates colliding (the Himalayas). A ridge with new sea floor matches plates moving apart. Earthquakes with no volcanoes match plates sliding past each other.
why: These features match two continental plates colliding, the Himalaya row. The new boundary has an ocean plate sinking, not two continents.
A ridge with new sea floor matches plates moving apart, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge row. The new boundary has plates moving together.
Earthquakes with no volcanoes match plates sliding past each other. A sinking ocean plate melts and feeds volcanoes.

items.prompt: At the rate given in the passage, about how many years will it take for the North American and Eurasian plates to move 1 meter farther apart?
items.hint: Convert 1 meter to centimeters first. Then divide distance by rate.
items.explain:
Step 1: Convert units. 1 m = 100 cm.

Step 2: time = distance ÷ rate = 100 cm ÷ 2.5 cm per year = 40 years.

A common error is dividing 1 by 2.5 without converting meters to centimeters, which gives 0.4.

mistakes.why: You divided 1 by 2.5 without converting units. The rate is in centimeters, so 1 m must become 100 cm: 100 ÷ 2.5 = 40.
You multiplied 100 cm by 2.5. That gives a distance, not a time. Time = distance ÷ rate = 100 ÷ 2.5 = 40.
You converted 1 m to 10 cm. There are 100 cm in a meter: 100 ÷ 2.5 = 40.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: Temperature fell after the eruption, hit its low a year later, and recovered within about four years.
The eruption caused a permanent drop in global average temperature that lasted through the last year shown.
Global average temperature rose by 0.4°C in the year after the eruption, then fell back to the earlier average.
The eruption had no measurable effect on global temperature, which was 0.0 both before and four years after.
items.hint: Look at the sign of each value and at what happens by the last year in the table.
items.explain:
The changes are 0.0 in the eruption year, then −0.4, −0.3, −0.1, and back to 0.0 four years after. The largest drop (−0.4°C) came one year after the eruption, and the temperature returned to the earlier average by year 4.

The drop was not permanent (it returned to 0.0). The value −0.4 is a decrease, not a rise. And a 0.4°C drop is a clear, measurable effect.
why: Look at the last row: 4 years after the eruption the change is back to 0.0. The cooling did not last.
The value is −0.4, not +0.4. The minus sign means the temperature fell below the earlier average.
You may have compared only the first and last rows, which are both 0.0. In between, temperature dropped as much as 0.4°C, a clear effect.

items.prompt:
Complete the explanation of the data.

The high haze of tiny droplets {{0}} part of the incoming sunlight back into space. As a result, less energy reached Earth's surface, and global average temperature {{1}} for a few years.

options: reflected
trapped
created
why: Trapping heat is what greenhouse gases do, and it causes warming. The data show cooling, so the haze must have sent sunlight away.
The haze cannot create sunlight. It can only change how much sunlight reaches the surface.

options: decreased
increased
stayed the same
why: The table shows negative changes after the eruption, which means temperature went down, not up.
The values change from 0.0 to −0.4, so temperature did not stay the same.

items.hint: The data show cooling. What must the haze have done with sunlight to cause cooling?
items.explain:
The table shows global temperature decreased after the eruption. Cooling means less of the Sun's energy reached the surface, so the haze must have reflected some sunlight back to space.

"Trapped" describes greenhouse gases, which hold heat in and cause warming, the opposite of what the data show. The haze does not "create" sunlight.

items.prompt:
Rock deep in the mantle, near the core, is heated. It becomes slightly less dense and slowly rises. Cooler rock near the top of the mantle is denser and slowly sinks. Scientists think this circulation helps move tectonic plates.

Which statement correctly identifies the heat transfer described?
options: Convection, because heated material rises and cooler material sinks.
Conduction, because heat passes from one rock particle to the next one touching it.
Radiation, because heat travels outward from the core as electromagnetic waves.
Convection, because heat naturally moves from cooler places toward warmer places.
why: Conduction moves heat through touching particles while the material stays in place. Here the rock itself rises and sinks, carrying heat with it.
Radiation carries energy as waves, like sunlight crossing space. The passage describes heated material physically moving.
The name is right but the reason is backward. Heat flows from warmer places to cooler places, never the reverse on its own.
items.hint: Is the heat passed along through touching material, carried as waves, or carried by material that moves?
items.explain: When a fluid or slowly flowing solid is heated from below, the warm material becomes less dense and rises while cooler, denser material sinks. That circulating flow is convection, the same process that moves warm air up from a heater. The tempting option names convection but gives a backward reason: heat always flows from warmer to cooler.

items.prompt: Which two statements are supported by the data in the table? Select two answers.
options: Planets farther from the Sun take longer to orbit the Sun.
A planet's mean temperature always decreases as its distance from the Sun increases.
Venus has a higher mean surface temperature than Mercury, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.
Mars takes less than one Earth year to orbit the Sun.
Jupiter's orbit takes about 5 times as long as Earth's orbit.
items.hint: Check each statement against every row. One counterexample is enough to make an "always" statement false.
items.explain:
Supported: Orbit times increase steadily as distance increases (0.24, 0.62, 1.00, 1.88, 11.86, 29.46 years). Venus (464°C) is hotter than Mercury (167°C) even though Venus is farther from the Sun.

Not supported: Temperature does not always decrease with distance; Venus breaks the pattern. Mars takes 1.88 Earth years, which is more than one. Jupiter's orbit takes 11.86 years, about 12 times Earth's, not 5 times. (The number 5 is close to Jupiter's distance, 5.20 AU, which is a different column.)
why: Venus breaks this pattern: it is farther from the Sun than Mercury but much hotter (464°C vs. 167°C). One exception makes an "always" statement false.
Mars takes 1.88 Earth years to orbit, which is more than one Earth year, not less.
Jupiter's orbit takes 11.86 years, about 12 times Earth's. The number 5 comes from Jupiter's distance column (5.20 AU), not its orbit time.

items.prompt: Earth is about 3% closer to the Sun in early January than in early July. Yet the Northern Hemisphere has winter in January and summer in July. Which statement best explains why the Northern Hemisphere is warmer in July?
options: In July, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, so it receives more direct sunlight and has longer days.
In July, Earth is closer to the Sun than at any other time of year, so the whole planet receives more energy.
The Sun gives off more energy in July than it does in January, so more heat reaches the Northern Hemisphere.
Earth spins faster in July, so each place in the Northern Hemisphere faces the Sun for more hours each day.
items.hint: The question already tells you that distance cannot be the reason.
items.explain:
Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°. In July, the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun. Sunlight strikes it more directly (concentrating energy on a smaller area) and days are longer, so it warms up.

The prompt states Earth is actually closer to the Sun in January, so distance cannot explain July warmth. The Sun's output does not swing between seasons, and Earth's rotation speed does not change with the seasons.
why: The prompt says Earth is actually closer to the Sun in January. If distance controlled the seasons, January would be the warm month.
The Sun's energy output stays nearly constant through the year. It does not rise in July.
Earth's rotation speed stays the same all year. Longer summer days come from the tilt, not faster spinning.

items.skill: Energy in food chains (life science review)
items.prompt:
A drought lowers the water in a pond. That summer, the algae in the pond capture only 50,000 kJ of energy from sunlight. Insect larvae eat the algae, small fish eat the larvae, and herons eat the small fish.

Using the 10% rule, about how many kilojoules of this energy reach the herons?

mistakes.why: 500 kJ reaches the small fish. The herons are one more step up: 500 × 0.10 = 50.
5,000 kJ is what reaches the insect larvae after one step. There are three steps from algae to herons.
You subtracted 10% at each step. The rule is that only about 10% passes up: multiply by 0.10, not 0.90.

items.hint: Count the arrows from algae to herons. Multiply by 0.10 once for each arrow.
items.explain:
Algae → larvae: 50,000 × 0.10 = 5,000 kJ.

Larvae → small fish: 5,000 × 0.10 = 500 kJ.

Small fish → herons: 500 × 0.10 = 50 kJ.

A common error is stopping at 500 kJ, the energy in the small fish. Count three arrows.

items.prompt: An earthquake sends out P-waves and S-waves at the same moment. P-waves travel through rock at about 7 km/s, and S-waves travel at about 4 km/s. A seismic station is 280 km from the earthquake. About how many seconds after the P-waves arrive will the S-waves arrive?
options: 30 seconds
40 seconds
70 seconds
110 seconds
why: 40 seconds is how long the P-waves take (280 ÷ 7). The question asks for the gap between the two arrivals.
70 seconds is how long the S-waves take (280 ÷ 4). Subtract the P-wave time to find the gap.
You added the two travel times (40 + 70). The gap between arrivals is the difference: 70 − 40.
items.hint: Find each wave's travel time with time = distance ÷ speed, then compare.
items.explain:
P-wave time: 280 km ÷ 7 km/s = 40 s.

S-wave time: 280 km ÷ 4 km/s = 70 s.

Gap: 70 − 40 = 30 seconds.

40 s and 70 s are the separate travel times, not the gap, and 110 s comes from adding instead of subtracting.

items.prompt:
A geologist finds a dark rock near an old lava flow. The rock has a mass of 135 g. She places it in a graduated cylinder holding 50.0 mL of water, and the water level rises to 100.0 mL.

What is the density of the rock in g/cm3? (1 mL = 1 cm3)

mistakes.why: You divided by the final water level, 100.0 mL. The rock's volume is only the rise in water: 100.0 − 50.0 = 50.0 mL.
You divided volume by mass. Density is mass divided by volume: 135 ÷ 50.0 = 2.7.
You multiplied mass by volume. Density = mass ÷ volume = 135 ÷ 50.0 = 2.7.

items.hint: The rock's volume is how much the water level rose. Then use density = mass ÷ volume.
items.explain:
Volume of rock = 100.0 mL − 50.0 mL = 50.0 mL = 50.0 cm3.

Density = mass ÷ volume = 135 g ÷ 50.0 cm3 = 2.7 g/cm3.

The tempting error is dividing by 100.0 mL, the final reading, which includes the water that was already there.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the results of the BTB experiment?
options: In light the plant removed carbon dioxide from the water, but in the dark it added carbon dioxide.
The plant carried out photosynthesis in both light and dark, removing carbon dioxide each time.
The snail removed carbon dioxide from the water, which is why Tube 3 stayed blue in the light.
Animals give off carbon dioxide, but plants never give off carbon dioxide under any conditions.
why: Tube 4 contradicts this. The plant in the dark turned the BTB yellow, so it added carbon dioxide; without light there is no photosynthesis.
Tube 1 shows the snail adds carbon dioxide (it turned yellow). Tube 3 stayed blue because the plant in light removed the carbon dioxide.
Tube 4 shows a plant in the dark does give off carbon dioxide. Plants carry out cellular respiration all the time, just like animals.
items.hint: Compare Tube 2 with Tube 4. What is the only difference, and what happened to the color?
items.explain:
Tube 1 (snail) turned yellow: the snail added CO2 by respiration. Tube 2 (plant, light) stayed blue: photosynthesis used CO2. Tube 4 (plant, dark) turned yellow: with no light there is no photosynthesis, but the plant's respiration still added CO2. So in light the plant removed CO2, and in the dark it added CO2.

The tempting choice, photosynthesis in both light and dark, ignores Tube 4. Photosynthesis needs light.

items.prompt: Which layer of Earth is the thickest and is made of hot, solid rock that flows very slowly?
options: Mantle
Crust
Outer core
Inner core
why: The crust is the thinnest layer, only about 5 to 70 km thick. It is the solid rock we live on.
The outer core is liquid iron and nickel, not slowly flowing rock.
The inner core is solid metal and the smallest layer, with a radius of about 1,200 km.
items.hint: This layer lies between the crust and the core.
items.explain: The mantle is nearly 2,900 km thick, the thickest layer. It is hot, solid rock that flows very slowly over long periods, which helps move the plates above it. The crust is thin, and both core layers are metal (the outer one liquid).

items.prompt: Which statement describes climate rather than weather?
options: A desert city receives an average of 8 inches of rain per year.
A thunderstorm dropped 2 inches of rain on the city yesterday afternoon.
Tomorrow's high temperature is expected to be 95°F.
Strong winds are forecast for this weekend.
items.hint: Climate describes a long-term average; weather describes hours or days.
items.explain:
An average yearly rainfall describes the long-term pattern of a place, which is climate.

The other three statements describe conditions over a single afternoon, a single day, or a weekend. Those are short-term conditions, so they describe weather.
why: A thunderstorm on one afternoon is a short-term condition, so it is weather.
A forecast for tomorrow describes one day's conditions: weather.
Winds forecast for one weekend are short-term conditions: weather.

items.prompt: Sort each description into the type of rock it forms.
choices: Lava cools so quickly that it hardens into glassy obsidian.
Rounded pebbles and sand are buried and cemented into conglomerate.
Limestone is heated and squeezed into marble without melting.
Magma cools slowly deep underground and forms granite with large crystals.
Layers of dead plant material are buried and pressed into coal.
Granite is changed into banded gneiss by intense heat and pressure.
items.why: The most common mistake is putting "Granite is changed into banded gneiss" in igneous because granite is igneous. The rock is named for its most recent change: heat and pressure without melting make gneiss metamorphic.
items.hint: Cooled melted rock = igneous. Pieces pressed and cemented in layers = sedimentary. Heat and pressure without melting = metamorphic.
items.explain:
Igneous: obsidian (lava cooled fast) and granite (magma cooled slowly). Both start as melted rock.

Sedimentary: conglomerate (pebbles and sand cemented) and coal (buried plant layers pressed together).

Metamorphic: marble (from limestone) and gneiss (from granite). Both are existing rocks changed by heat and pressure without melting.

items.prompt: In guinea pigs, the allele for black fur (B) is dominant over the allele for white fur (b). A guinea pig with genotype Bb is crossed with one with genotype bb. What is the probability that an offspring will have white fur?
why: You may have assumed a black parent always passes on black fur. The Bb parent passes on b half the time, and the bb parent always passes on b.
25% is the answer for a Bb × Bb cross. Here one parent is bb, so two of the four boxes are bb.
75% is the chance of the dominant trait in a Bb × Bb cross. In this cross, black and white are each 2 of 4 boxes.
items.hint: Draw a 2-by-2 Punnett square with B and b on one side and b and b on the other.
items.explain:
Punnett square for Bb × bb: the four boxes are Bb, Bb, bb, bb.

White fur needs bb: 2 of 4 boxes = 50%.

25% is the tempting answer if you treat this like the Bb × Bb cross from class; check both parents' genotypes before drawing the square.

items.prompt: Scientists study a newly mapped boundary where two plates are moving apart. Based on the table, which set of features would they most likely find there?
options: Rift valleys, volcanic eruptions, shallow earthquakes, and new crust forming
Deep ocean trenches, many active volcanoes, and quakes that can cause tsunamis
High, folded mountains and earthquakes, with no active volcanoes
Frequent strong earthquakes along one fault, with no volcanoes nearby
why: These features match Japan, where ocean plates sink beneath another plate. Plates moving apart do not form trenches.
These features match the Alps, where two continental plates push together.
These features match the North Anatolian Fault, where plates slide past each other.
items.hint: Find the row in the table with the same plate motion.
items.explain:
Iceland is the row where two plates move apart. Its features are rift valleys, volcanic eruptions, small shallow earthquakes, and new crust, so a boundary with the same motion would most likely show the same features.

Trenches and tsunami-causing quakes match sinking plates (Japan); folded mountains match colliding continents (the Alps); a single active fault with no volcanoes matches sliding plates (Turkey).

items.prompt: A fence was built straight across the transform fault described below the table. At the rate given, how many years will it take for the two halves of the fence to be offset by 6 meters?

mistakes.why: You divided 6 by 4 without converting. The rate is in centimeters, so 6 m must become 600 cm: 600 ÷ 4 = 150.
You multiplied 600 cm by 4. That does not give a time. Time = distance ÷ rate = 600 ÷ 4 = 150.
You converted 6 m to 60 cm. There are 100 cm in a meter, so 6 m = 600 cm, and 600 ÷ 4 = 150.

items.hint: Convert 6 meters to centimeters first. Then divide by the rate.
items.explain:
Step 1: 6 m × 100 = 600 cm.

Step 2: time = distance ÷ rate = 600 cm ÷ 4 cm per year = 150 years.

A common error is dividing 6 by 4 without converting, which gives 1.5.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: In this test, steeper trays lost more soil: 42 g at 10° but 231 g at 40°.
Soil loss doubled each time the student raised the tray angle by another 10°.
Steeper trays lost less soil, because the water ran off them too fast to carry it.
Slope angle is the only factor that controls how much soil a hillside loses to rain.
items.hint: Test each statement against the actual numbers in the table. Watch for claims that go beyond what was tested.
items.explain:
Soil loss rose at every step as the angle increased: 42, 95, 160, 231 g. So in this test, steeper trays lost more soil.

It did not double each time: 42 × 2 = 84 (actual 95), 95 × 2 = 190 (actual 160), 160 × 2 = 320 (actual 231). And the experiment changed only one factor (tray angle, the independent variable), so it cannot show that slope is the only cause of erosion; rainfall, plant cover, and soil type also matter.
why: Check the numbers: 42 × 2 = 84 (actual 95), 95 × 2 = 190 (actual 160), 160 × 2 = 320 (actual 231). Soil loss rose, but it did not double each time.
This reverses the data. Soil loss went up at every step (42, 95, 160, 231 g), so steeper trays lost more soil, not less.
This goes beyond the data. The student tested only one factor, so the results cannot show that slope is the only cause; rainfall, plant cover, and soil type also affect erosion.

items.prompt:
Complete the explanation.

Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas: it {{0}} heat given off by Earth's surface. From 1960 to 2020, the amount of carbon dioxide in the air {{1}}. Because more greenhouse gas traps more heat, this trend is expected to make Earth's average temperature {{2}}.

options: absorbs
reflects
creates
why: Reflecting incoming sunlight is what a volcanic haze or bright clouds do, which causes cooling. Greenhouse gases absorb the heat leaving Earth's surface.
Gases cannot create energy. Greenhouse gases absorb heat that Earth's surface gives off.

options: rose in every decade
rose and then fell
stayed about the same
fell in every decade
why: Every value in the table is higher than the one before it (317, 326, 339, 354, 370, 390, 414). There is no decline.
The level rose from 317 to 414 ppm, an increase of 97 ppm. That is not “about the same.”
You may have read the table backward. Later years have higher values, not lower.

options: rise
fall
stay the same
why: More heat-trapping gas holds more heat near the surface, which warms Earth rather than cooling it.
If more heat is trapped, the temperature cannot stay the same; it goes up.

items.hint: Read every value in the table from left to right. Then think about what trapping more heat does.
items.explain:
Greenhouse gases absorb the heat (infrared energy) given off by Earth's surface and send some back down. The table shows carbon dioxide rose in every decade: 317, 326, 339, 354, 370, 390, 414 ppm. More greenhouse gas traps more heat, so Earth's average temperature is expected to rise.

"Reflects" is the tempting wrong choice: that describes volcanic haze, which bounces sunlight away and cools Earth.

items.prompt:
On a sunny afternoon, land near a beach heats up faster than the ocean. The air above the land warms and rises, and cooler air from over the water moves in to take its place. This creates a steady sea breeze.

Which statement correctly identifies the heat transfer that moves the air?
options: Convection, because warm air rises and cooler air flows in to replace it.
Conduction, because the warm sand touches the layer of air just above it.
Radiation, because the Sun's energy travels to the beach as light waves.
Convection, because cool air rises over the water and warm air sinks over land.
why: Conduction does warm the thin layer of air touching the sand, but the breeze itself is air moving in a loop. Moving fluid that carries heat is convection.
Radiation is how sunlight heats the land in the first place, but it does not move the air. The breeze is warm air rising and cool air flowing in.
The name is right but the description is reversed. Warm, less dense air rises over the land; cooler, denser air sinks and flows in.
items.hint: The question asks what moves the air, not what heats the sand.
items.explain: Warm air over the land is less dense, so it rises. Cooler, denser air from over the ocean flows in underneath. That circulating motion of a fluid is convection. Radiation from the Sun heats the land, and conduction warms the air touching the sand, but the breeze itself is convection. The tempting option names convection but reverses which air rises.

items.prompt: Which two statements are supported by the data in the table? Select two answers.
options: Each of the four inner planets has a smaller diameter than each of the four outer planets.
Mercury and Mars have the same surface gravity, even though Mars has a larger diameter.
A planet's surface gravity always increases as its diameter increases.
Neptune is about twice as far from the Sun as Saturn.
A person would weigh less on Jupiter than on Earth.
why: Saturn is more than twice as wide as Neptune (120,536 km vs. 49,528 km) but has weaker surface gravity (9.0 vs. 11.0). One exception makes "always" false.
4,515 ÷ 1,432 ≈ 3.2, so Neptune is about three times as far from the Sun as Saturn, not twice.
Jupiter's surface gravity (23.1 m/s<sup>2</sup>) is more than twice Earth's (9.8), so a person would weigh more there.
items.hint: Test each statement against every row. One counterexample is enough to make an "always" statement false.
items.explain:
Supported: The largest inner planet, Earth (12,756 km), is smaller than the smallest outer planet, Neptune (49,528 km). Mercury and Mars both have a surface gravity of 3.7 m/s2, though Mars is wider (6,792 km vs. 4,879 km).

Not supported: Gravity does not always rise with diameter (Saturn vs. Neptune). Neptune is about 3.2 times as far as Saturn. Jupiter's stronger gravity would make a person weigh more, not less.

items.prompt: In December, people in Australia enjoy summer while people in Canada have winter. Which statement best explains why?
options: The Southern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun in December, so it gets more direct sunlight and longer days.
Earth is closest to the Sun in December, so the half of Earth that faces the Sun at that time becomes much warmer.
The Sun sends more of its energy toward the Southern Hemisphere than toward the Northern Hemisphere in December.
Earth's rotation slows down in December, so places in Australia face the Sun for more hours each day.
why: If distance caused the seasons, both hemispheres would warm at the same time. Instead, Canada has winter in December. (Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January.)
The Sun shines in all directions equally. What changes is the angle at which its light strikes each hemisphere, because of Earth's tilt.
Earth's rotation speed stays the same all year. Longer summer days in Australia come from the tilt of Earth's axis.
items.hint: If both hemispheres are the same distance from the Sun, what is different about them in December?
items.explain:
Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°. In December the Southern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun: sunlight strikes it more directly, concentrating energy on a smaller area, and days are longer, so Australia has summer. At the same time the Northern Hemisphere leans away, so Canada has winter.

The distance explanation fails because it would give both hemispheres the same season at the same time.

items.skill: Energy in food chains (life science review)
items.prompt:
Grasses in a prairie store 80,000 kJ of energy. Grasshoppers eat the grasses, frogs eat the grasshoppers, and snakes eat the frogs.

Using the 10% rule, about how many kilojoules of this energy reach the snakes?

mistakes.why: 800 kJ reaches the frogs. The snakes are one more step up: 800 × 0.10 = 80.
You took 10% four times. Count the arrows: grasses → grasshoppers → frogs → snakes is three steps.
You subtracted 10% at each step. Only about 10% passes up each level, so multiply by 0.10, not 0.90.

items.hint: Count the arrows from grasses to snakes. Multiply by 0.10 once for each arrow.
items.explain:
Grasses → grasshoppers: 80,000 × 0.10 = 8,000 kJ.

Grasshoppers → frogs: 8,000 × 0.10 = 800 kJ.

Frogs → snakes: 800 × 0.10 = 80 kJ.

A common error is stopping at 800 kJ, the energy in the frogs. Count three arrows.

items.prompt: An earthquake sends out two kinds of waves at the same moment. P-waves travel through rock at about 6 km/s, and S-waves travel at about 3.5 km/s. A seismic station is 210 km from the earthquake. About how many seconds after the P-waves arrive will the S-waves arrive?
options: 25 seconds
35 seconds
60 seconds
95 seconds
items.hint: Find the travel time of each wave with time = distance ÷ speed, then subtract.
items.explain:
P-wave time: 210 km ÷ 6 km/s = 35 s.

S-wave time: 210 km ÷ 3.5 km/s = 60 s.

Difference: 60 − 35 = 25 seconds.

35 s and 60 s are the separate travel times, not the gap between them. 95 s comes from adding the two times instead of subtracting.
why: 35 seconds is how long the P-waves take (210 ÷ 6). The question asks for the gap between the two arrivals.
60 seconds is how long the S-waves take (210 ÷ 3.5). Subtract the P-wave time to find the gap.
You added the two travel times (35 + 60). The gap between arrivals is the difference: 60 − 35.

items.prompt:
A student collects a light-gray rock on a hike. The rock has a mass of 92 g. She lowers it into a graduated cylinder holding 30.0 mL of water, and the water level rises to 70.0 mL.

What is the density of the rock in g/cm3? (1 mL = 1 cm3)

mistakes.why: You divided by the final water level, 70.0 mL. The rock's volume is only the rise: 70.0 − 30.0 = 40.0 mL.
You divided by the starting water level, 30.0 mL. The rock's volume is the rise in water: 70.0 − 30.0 = 40.0 mL.
You divided volume by mass. Density is mass divided by volume: 92 ÷ 40.0 = 2.3.

items.hint: The rock's volume is how much the water level rose. Then use density = mass ÷ volume.
items.explain:
Volume of rock = 70.0 mL − 30.0 mL = 40.0 mL = 40.0 cm3.

Density = mass ÷ volume = 92 g ÷ 40.0 cm3 = 2.3 g/cm3.

The tempting error is dividing by 70.0 mL, the final reading, which includes the water already in the cylinder.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the greenhouse data?
options: In daylight the plants took in more carbon dioxide than they released; at night they released it.
The plants carried out respiration only during the day and photosynthesis only at night.
Carbon dioxide in the greenhouse was highest around noon, when sunlight was strongest.
The plants stopped carrying out cellular respiration completely during the daylight hours.
why: This reverses the two processes. Photosynthesis needs light, so it happens in the day; the CO<sub>2</sub> rise at night comes from respiration.
Read the noon value again: 350 ppm is one of the lowest readings. CO<sub>2</sub> was highest at about sunrise (450 ppm at 6 a.m.).
The data show only the overall change. A falling CO<sub>2</sub> level means photosynthesis used more than respiration released; it does not show respiration stopped.
items.hint: When does the CO<sub>2</sub> level fall, and when does it rise? Which process uses CO<sub>2</sub>, and which needs light?
items.explain:
From 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., CO2 fell from 450 to 325 ppm: in daylight, photosynthesis used more CO2 than respiration gave off. After sunset (about 7 p.m.), CO2 rose again, reaching 440 ppm by 3 a.m.: in the dark there is no photosynthesis, and respiration adds CO2.

The tempting choice, that respiration stopped during the day, goes beyond the data. Plants respire all the time; the drop only shows that photosynthesis outpaced respiration.

items.prompt: Earthquake S-waves can travel through solid rock but cannot travel through liquid. Seismic stations on the far side of Earth from a large earthquake do not detect S-waves coming straight through the planet. Which layer most likely blocks them?
options: Outer core
Inner core
Mantle
Crust
why: The inner core is solid, so it would not stop S-waves. The waves are stopped before they ever reach it, by the liquid layer around it.
This answer comes from the misconception that the mantle is liquid magma. The mantle is solid rock, so S-waves pass through it.
The crust is solid rock. S-waves travel through it easily, which is how they reach nearby stations.
items.hint: Which layer is the only liquid one?
items.explain: S-waves cannot pass through liquid. The outer core is Earth's only liquid layer, so it blocks S-waves from reaching the far side of the planet. items.prompt: Which type of plate boundary best explains the features and data described?
options: A convergent boundary where an ocean plate sinks beneath a continental plate
A divergent boundary where two plates pull apart and magma rises between them
A transform boundary where two plates slide horizontally past each other
A convergent boundary where two continental plates collide and crumple upward
why: Volcanoes alone might suggest plates pulling apart, but divergent boundaries make ridges and rift valleys, not trenches, and their earthquakes stay shallow.
Transform boundaries cause earthquakes, but they do not form trenches or chains of volcanoes, and their earthquakes stay shallow.
This is the right kind of motion but the wrong plates. Two colliding continents build tall mountains with few volcanoes and no ocean trench.
items.hint: Use all three clues: the trench, the volcanoes, and the way earthquake depth changes inland.
items.explain: A deep trench offshore, a chain of volcanoes inland, and earthquakes that get deeper inland (20 km, 60 km, 110 km, 160 km) all point to an ocean plate sinking beneath a continental plate. The deepening earthquakes trace the sinking plate as it dives into the mantle, and melting above it feeds the volcanoes. Two colliding continents would build mountains with few volcanoes and no trench.

items.prompt: At the rate given, how many kilometers of the ocean plate will move toward the coast in 1 million years?

mistakes.why: 80,000 is the distance in meters. Divide by 1,000 to change meters to kilometers: 80 km.
8,000,000 is the distance in centimeters. Convert: ÷ 100 gives meters (80,000), then ÷ 1,000 gives kilometers (80).
You divided by only 10,000. There are 100,000 cm in a kilometer: 8,000,000 ÷ 100,000 = 80.

items.explain:
distance = rate × time = 8 cm/year × 1,000,000 years = 8,000,000 cm.

8,000,000 cm ÷ 100 = 80,000 m.

80,000 m ÷ 1,000 = 80 km.

items.prompt: Layers W, X, Y, and Z are sedimentary rock. V is igneous rock that formed when magma pushed up into cracks and hardened. Put the events in order from oldest to youngest.

figure.alt: Rock layers stacked from bottom to top: Layer W, Layer X, Layer Y, Layer Z. A band of igneous rock labeled V cuts upward through Layers W and X and stops at the bottom of Layer Y.

items.why: The most common mistake is placing intrusion V last because it cuts across rock. V cuts only W and X; layers Y and Z lie unbroken on top of it, so they formed after V.
items.explain:
By superposition, the sedimentary layers formed from the bottom up: W, then X. V cuts through W and X, so it is younger than both. V stops at the bottom of Y, so Y and then Z were deposited after V hardened.

Order: W, X, V, Y, Z.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: Seaport's yearly range is about one-third of Plainsville's, so the ocean likely moderates it.
Plainsville is warmer than Seaport in every month shown, because it is farther inland.
The two cities have about the same yearly range, because they are at the same latitude.
Plainsville's yearly range is 21°C, which is only a little larger than Seaport's range.
why: Check January and October: Plainsville (−6°C and 11°C) is colder than Seaport (8°C and 15°C) in both.
Latitude is the same, but the ranges are very different: 11°C for Seaport and 33°C for Plainsville. Distance from the ocean matters too.
You subtracted 6 instead of −6. Plainsville's range is 27 − (−6) = 33°C, three times Seaport's 11°C.
items.explain:
Seaport's range: 19 − 8 = 11°C. Plainsville's range: 27 − (−6) = 33°C. Seaport's range is one-third of Plainsville's. Water heats and cools slowly (high specific heat), so the ocean keeps Seaport cooler in summer and warmer in winter.

The tempting error is computing Plainsville's range as 27 − 6 = 21°C, which ignores the negative sign.

items.prompt: In one year, a region had a magnitude 7.2 earthquake and a magnitude 5.2 earthquake. How many times greater was the ground shaking (wave amplitude) of the larger earthquake?

mistakes.why: 2 is the difference in magnitude, the number of steps. Each step multiplies shaking by 10: 10 × 10 = 100.
You multiplied 10 by 2. Each step multiplies again: 10 × 10 = 100.
That is the energy comparison (32 × 32 ≈ 1,000). The question asks about shaking, which grows 10 times per step: 100.

items.explain:
Difference: 7.2 − 5.2 = 2 steps.

Shaking: 10 × 10 = 100 times greater.

(The energy released would be about 32 × 32 ≈ 1,000 times greater, but the question asks about shaking.)

items.prompt: Which two statements are supported by the data? Select two answers.
options: Neptune takes more than 10 times as long as Jupiter to orbit the Sun.
For these four planets, mean temperature drops as distance from the Sun increases.
Uranus has a lower mean temperature than Neptune does.
Neptune is about 10 times as far from the Sun as Jupiter is.
Jupiter, the closest of the four, has the longest orbital period.
why: Uranus is −195°C and Neptune is −200°C. Neptune is colder; −200 is lower than −195.
4,515 ÷ 778.5 ≈ 5.8, so Neptune is about 6 times as far as Jupiter. The “more than 10 times” pattern belongs to the orbit times, not the distances.
Jupiter has the shortest orbital period (4,331 days). Closer planets have shorter years.
items.explain:
Supported: 59,800 ÷ 4,331 ≈ 13.8, so Neptune's orbit takes more than 10 times as long as Jupiter's. Temperatures fall in order of distance: −110, −140, −195, −200°C.

Not supported: Uranus (−195°C) is warmer than Neptune (−200°C). Neptune is about 5.8 times as far as Jupiter, not 10. Jupiter has the shortest orbital period, not the longest.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: More sugar raised gas output up to about 10 g; more than that added little gas.
Gas production doubled each time the amount of sugar in the bottle was doubled.
Yeast cannot give off any gas at all unless sugar is added to the warm water.
Gas production would keep rising steadily if 40 g of sugar were added to a bottle.
why: Check the doublings: 5 g to 10 g raised gas from 40 to 75 mL (not 80), and 10 g to 20 g raised it only from 75 to 79 mL.
The 0 g bottle still produced 5 mL of gas, so some gas formed without added sugar.
This goes beyond the data. From 10 g to 20 g the gas barely changed (75 to 79 mL), so the trend was leveling off, not rising steadily.
items.explain:
Gas rose quickly from 0 g to 10 g (5, 40, 75 mL), then barely changed from 10 g to 20 g (75, 78, 79 mL). So more sugar helped up to about 10 g, after which extra sugar added little gas.

The tempting choice about doubling fails when you check the numbers: doubling sugar from 10 g to 20 g added only 4 mL.

items.prompt: Which statement correctly compares Earth's inner core and outer core?
options: Both are mostly iron and nickel, but great pressure keeps the hotter inner core solid.
The inner core is made of liquid rock, and the outer core is made of solid metal.
The outer core is hotter than the inner core, and that extra heat is why it is liquid.
Both are solid rock that flows very slowly over time, just like the rock of the mantle.
why: This reverses the two layers. The outer core is the liquid one, and both cores are metal, not rock.
The inner core is actually the hotter layer. It stays solid because the pressure at Earth's center is so great.
That describes the mantle. Both core layers are iron and nickel, and the outer core is liquid.
items.explain: Both core layers are made mostly of iron and nickel. The outer core is liquid. The inner core is even hotter, but the enormous pressure at Earth's center keeps it solid. The tempting error is assuming the liquid layer must be the hotter one; pressure, not just temperature, decides whether the metal melts.

items.prompt: Which type of plate boundary best explains the features of Region R?
options: A divergent boundary where a continent is being pulled apart and magma rises
A convergent boundary where an ocean plate sinks beneath a continental plate
A transform boundary where two plates slide horizontally past each other
A convergent boundary where two continental plates collide and crumple upward
why: Volcanoes can form here too, but sinking plates make a deep trench and deep earthquakes. Region R has an opening valley and shallow earthquakes.
At a transform boundary the sides slide past each other; they do not move apart, and there are few or no volcanoes.
Colliding continents push crust up into mountains. Region R's valley is opening because the two sides are moving apart.
items.explain: The GPS data show the two sides moving away from each other, and a valley is opening, with volcanoes and shallow earthquakes. These are the signs of a divergent boundary on a continent (a rift valley). The sinking-plate option is tempting because of the volcanoes, but it would also produce a trench and deep earthquakes.

items.prompt: At the rate given, how many years will it take for the two sides of the valley to move 1.5 kilometers farther apart?

mistakes.why: You divided 1.5 by 3 without converting. The rate is in centimeters: 1.5 km = 150,000 cm, and 150,000 ÷ 3 = 50,000.
You converted 1.5 km to meters (1,500) but not to centimeters. 1.5 km = 150,000 cm; 150,000 ÷ 3 = 50,000.
You converted 1.5 km to 15,000 cm. There are 100,000 cm in a kilometer, so 1.5 km = 150,000 cm.

items.explain:
1.5 km × 1,000 = 1,500 m; 1,500 m × 100 = 150,000 cm.

time = distance ÷ rate = 150,000 cm ÷ 3 cm per year = 50,000 years.

items.prompt: Layers K, L, M, and N are sedimentary rock. J is igneous rock that formed when magma pushed up through cracks and hardened. Put the events in order from oldest to youngest.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 330 176' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='40' y='122' width='190' height='34' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><text x='242' y='144' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D'>Layer K</text><rect x='40' y='88' width='190' height='34' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><text x='242' y='110' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D'>Layer L</text><rect x='40' y='54' width='190' height='34' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><text x='242' y='76' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D'>Layer M</text><rect x='40' y='20' width='190' height='34' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><text x='242' y='42' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D'>Layer N</text><polygon points='120,156 142,156 146,54 126,54' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><text x='130' y='110' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D'>J</text></svg>
figure.alt: Rock layers stacked from bottom to top: Layer K, Layer L, Layer M, Layer N. A band of igneous rock labeled J cuts upward through Layers K, L, and M and stops at the bottom of Layer N.

items.why: The most common mistake is placing intrusion J last because it cuts across rock. J cuts only K, L, and M; layer N lies unbroken on top of it, so N formed after J.
items.explain:
By superposition, the sedimentary layers formed from the bottom up: K, then L, then M. J cuts through K, L, and M, so it is younger than all three. J stops at the bottom of N, so N was deposited after J hardened.

Order: K, L, M, J, N.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the information?
options: The decade averages rose 1.0°C in all, and one cold month does not reverse that trend.
The record-cold January of 2019 shows that the city's climate is now growing colder.
The city's temperature rose by exactly the same amount every year from 1981 to 2020.
The data prove that the city's warming was caused entirely by its growing local traffic.
why: One cold month is weather. Climate is the long-term average, and every decade average was higher than the one before.
The table gives only decade averages, so it cannot show year-by-year changes. Even the decade increases differ (0.3, 0.4, 0.3°C).
The data show a trend, not its cause. Nothing in the table measures traffic, and data never “prove” a cause on their own.
items.explain:
The decade averages rose from 12.1°C to 13.1°C: 13.1 − 12.1 = 1.0°C. That long-term rise describes climate. One record-cold January is weather, a short-term event, and does not reverse a 40-year trend.

The tempting error is treating one memorable cold month as evidence about climate.

items.prompt: A magnitude 8.1 earthquake struck the same region as an earlier magnitude 5.1 earthquake. How many times greater was the ground shaking (wave amplitude) of the 8.1 earthquake?

mistakes.why: 3 is the difference in magnitude, the number of steps. Each step multiplies shaking by 10: 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000.
You multiplied 10 by 3. Each step multiplies again: 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000.
That is the energy comparison (32 × 32 × 32). The question asks about shaking, which grows 10 times per step: 1,000.

items.explain:
Difference: 8.1 − 5.1 = 3 steps.

Shaking: 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000 times greater.

items.prompt: Which two statements are supported by the data? Select two answers.
options: Mars takes nearly two Earth years to orbit the Sun.
Mercury orbits the Sun about four times in one Earth year.
Venus is the largest of the four inner planets.
Mars is about twice as far from the Sun as Earth is.
A planet's diameter increases as its distance from the Sun increases.
why: Earth (12,756 km) is slightly larger than Venus (12,104 km). Read both rows closely.
228.0 ÷ 149.6 ≈ 1.5, so Mars is about one and a half times as far as Earth, not twice.
Mars is farther from the Sun than Earth but much smaller (6,792 km vs. 12,756 km), so the pattern does not hold.
items.explain:
Supported: 687.0 ÷ 365.2 ≈ 1.9, so Mars takes nearly two Earth years. 365.2 ÷ 88.0 ≈ 4.2, so Mercury orbits about four times per Earth year.

Not supported: Earth, not Venus, is the largest inner planet. Mars is about 1.5 times as far as Earth. Diameter does not rise with distance (Mars is smaller than Earth).

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: Raising the ramp to about 30 cm increased distance; going higher added little.
The rolling distance doubled each time the height of the ramp was doubled.
The car cannot roll across the floor at all unless the ramp is at least 10 cm high.
The rolling distance would keep rising steadily if the ramp were raised to 100 cm.
why: This roughly holds from 10 to 20 cm (52 to 101 cm), but doubling from 20 to 40 cm raised the distance only from 101 to 160 cm, not 202.
No heights below 10 cm were tested, so the data cannot tell us what happens on lower ramps.
This goes beyond the data. From 30 to 50 cm the distance barely changed (148 to 163 cm), so the trend was leveling off.
items.explain:
Distance rose steeply from 10 to 30 cm of height (52, 101, 148 cm), then changed little from 30 to 50 cm (148, 160, 163 cm). So raising the ramp helped up to about 30 cm, after which extra height added little distance.

The tempting doubling claim nearly works for 10 to 20 cm but fails from 20 to 40 cm.

vocab.def: The theory that Earth's outer shell is broken into large plates that slowly move.
vocab.example: Plate movement explains why earthquakes cluster along certain coastlines.

vocab.def: The thick layer of hot, mostly solid rock between the crust and the core; it flows very slowly.
vocab.example: Heat currents in the mantle help move tectonic plates.

vocab.def: A place where two plates move apart and new crust forms.
A place where two plates push together, forming trenches, volcanoes, or mountains.
vocab.example: The collision that built the Himalayas.

vocab.def: A place where two plates slide past each other, causing earthquakes.
vocab.example: The North Anatolian Fault in Turkey, where the ground shifts sideways in earthquakes.

vocab.def: The ongoing process by which rocks change from one type (igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic) to another.
vocab.example: Granite weathers into sand, which becomes sandstone.

vocab.def: The movement of weathered rock and soil by water, wind, ice, or gravity.
vocab.example: A river carries mud downstream after a storm.

vocab.def: In undisturbed layers of sedimentary rock, the oldest layer is at the bottom and the youngest is at the top.
vocab.example: A fossil in a lower layer is generally older than a fossil in a layer above it.

vocab.def: The condition of the atmosphere at a place over hours or days.
The average weather pattern of a place over many years, usually 30 or more.
vocab.example: A desert climate with hot summers and little rain.

vocab.def: The warming of Earth's surface when gases in the atmosphere trap heat.
vocab.example: Carbon dioxide from burning fuel adds to the greenhouse effect.

vocab.def: A number that describes the size of an earthquake; each whole number up means about 10 times more shaking.
vocab.example: A magnitude 6 shakes about 10 times more than a magnitude 5.

vocab.def: A natural event that can harm people or property.
The force of attraction between objects with mass; it keeps planets in orbit around the Sun.
vocab.example: The Sun's gravity holds Earth in its yearly orbit.

vocab.def: The distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometers; used to measure distances to stars and galaxies.
vocab.example: A star 10 light-years away is seen by light that left it 10 years ago.

notes:
Study Notes: Earth and Space + Full Science Review

Earth's Layers (outside in)

Crust (thin, solid) → Mantle (thickest, mostly solid, flows slowly) → Outer core (liquid iron/nickel) → Inner core (solid, hottest)

Plate Boundaries

  • Divergent (apart): ridges, rift valleys, new crust
  • Convergent (together): trenches, volcanoes, mountains
  • Transform (slide past): earthquakes, faults

Rock Cycle

  • Igneous: magma/lava cools
  • Sedimentary: layers pressed and cemented; fossils
  • Metamorphic: heat + pressure, no melting

Rock layers: oldest at the bottom (superposition); rock that cuts across layers is younger than they are.

Weather, Climate, Seasons

  • Weather = short-term. Climate = long-term average (30+ years).
  • Seasons = Earth's 23.5° tilt, not distance.
  • Greenhouse gases (CO2, methane, water vapor) trap heat. CO2 at Mauna Loa: 317 ppm (1960) → 414 ppm (2020).
  • Water heats and cools slowly: coasts are milder.

Space

  • Sun = star; gravity holds 8 planets in orbit.
  • Inner = rocky; outer = gas giants. Farther = longer year.
  • Rotation = day/night. Revolution = 1 year.
  • Moon phases = our view of its lit half (29.5 days). Earth's shadow = eclipse, not a phase.
  • Light-year = distance light travels in 1 year.

Earthquake magnitude: +1 = 10× shaking, about 32× energy. +2 = 100× shaking. Hurricanes: Cat 1 = 74–95 mph … Cat 5 = 157+ mph. Earth's systems: geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere; a change in one affects the others.

FormulaUse
mean = sum ÷ countAverages, trials, climate data
speed (rate) = distance ÷ timeMotion, plate movement, seismic waves
density = mass ÷ volumeMatter, rocks, floating and sinking
force = mass × accelerationNewton's second law
work = force × distanceMachines and energy
Punnett square: 4 boxes, each 25%Probability of a trait
Food chain: about 10% of energy passes onEcosystems (multiply by 0.10 per arrow)
distance = rate × time (convert units first)Plate motion: 1 km = 100,000 cm

Watch out: weather ≠ climate. Summer is not caused by being closer to the Sun. Conclusions must stay inside the data.
